analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical makers to give the EPA reference samples for PFAS chemicals so they can be tested and regulated.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS "forever chemicals" are hard to test for because labs need a known pure sample — a reference standard — to measure them accurately. This bill would have required companies that manufacture PFAS to give the EPA a reference standard for every such chemical they have made in the last ten years. The EPA and states could use those samples to develop detection methods and enforce pollution rules, but not to sell them commercially. The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living near PFAS-contaminated water and sites, and state environmental agencies, gain better tools to detect and enforce limits on PFAS pollution, because labs can only accurately measure these chemicals when they have a known reference sample to compare against.

how_it_helps.text: It requires manufacturers to hand the EPA a verified reference sample — an analytical reference standard — for each PFAS chemical they made in the past ten years, which is the raw material needed for reliable lab testing.
It lets the EPA and state governments use those samples to develop testing protocols and enforce federal and state requirements, and bars anyone from selling the samples commercially.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers pay a compliance cost: they must produce and submit a certified reference standard for each PFAS chemical they made in the past decade.

drawbacks.text: The compliance requirement falls on manufacturers, who would bear the cost of producing and submitting reference standards for every PFAS chemical they made in the past ten years, and the bill sets a 180-day deadline that could be demanding for companies with large chemical portfolios.

The bill only requires submission of standards; it does not itself set limits on PFAS in water or products, so on its own it strengthens testing and enforcement tools rather than directly restricting pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — making it possible to identify and enforce limits on PFAS chemicals polluting drinking water and communities — far outweighs the cost, which is a compliance task for manufacturers. The bill's weakness was procedural, not substantive: it was introduced late in the session and went no further.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired with the Congress.

narrative.text: Representative John Sarbanes introduced the PFAS Reference Standards Act on May 27, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action was ever taken — the bill received no subcommittee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

The bill would have required PFAS manufacturers to give the EPA an analytical reference standard for each such chemical they made in the prior ten years, a sample labs need to reliably detect the chemicals in water, soil, and blood.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers are better off: the tools the EPA would have gained for detecting and enforcing limits on their chemicals never became law.

for.name: 8 House cosponsors (6 Democrats, 2 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill a small bipartisan base.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up — no hearing, markup, or vote was recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a modest bipartisan group of cosponsors (6 Democrats and 2 Republicans), but it never reached a vote, so no party breakdown on the merits exists.

industries.note: The bill requires manufacturers to submit reference standards for PFAS they have made in the past decade, aiding oversight and enforcement against them. PFAS exposure has been linked to serious health harms, so the industry's interest runs against the public's in this bill.
Testing labs, states, and water systems benefit from better reference standards, which make detection and enforcement of PFAS limits more accurate and defensible.
